metadata.title: Claude, Claim Chart.
metadata.purpose: Answer what a finished claim chart actually proves: is a chart with every cell filled in the strong version of it? Lands the carry-out that the chart's job is a pin cite for what's supported and a flag, element by element, for what's missing.
metadata.source_note: Unlike sibling redos in this family (amendment-history, ai-inventory), the source sheet's narration carried REAL facts, not unfilled placeholders: claim-chart builds/reviews an element chart (patent claim chart or civil element chart), every cell pin-cited, gap detection as the priority output. See QUESTION.md.

beats.narration_text: Someone asked whether a filled claim chart proves the case. Wrong verb. The chart doesn't prove — it maps, element by element, where the evidence lands and, just as importantly, where it doesn't.

beats.narration_text: Here's how the chart actually works. A legal claim decomposes into elements, and each element needs its own proof. Draw the grid — one row per element, one column for the citation — and the tempting read is completeness: every box has an entry, every element must be covered. That read is wrong. A filled cell only records that someone found a citation. It says nothing about whether that citation actually proves the element it sits under.

shot.new_visual_element: A chart grid filling in, cell by cell, each one glowing 'covered' as it fills

production_viz.label: A full grid reads as a strong case
production_viz.mechanic: A claim chart grid: rows are elements, one column. Cells fill left to right, each landing with a soft 'COVERED' stamp. The whole grid fills, looking complete. A caption fades in beneath: 'a filled cell only shows a citation was found.'

beats.narration_text: Watch the routine execute, element by element. For every element, the chart hunts the source for a passage that could support it and pin-cites the exact page and line. Two elements from the same claim, same manual. 'A locking mechanism' turns up a citation straight to the product manual, page twelve. 'A temperature sensor' turns up nothing in that manual — no passage matches, so no citation goes in the cell.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR -- two element rows on one chart: one cell fills with a pin cite, the other stays empty, flagged

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR -- one cited, one gapped
production_viz.mechanic: Two rows of one chart: 'A LOCKING MECHANISM' fills with 'MANUAL, P.12' pin-cited beneath it. 'A TEMPERATURE SENSOR' stays empty, then a terracotta 'GAP' tag drops in beneath it. THIS EXACT TWO-ROW CHART RETURNS, RESOLVED, AT B03.

beats.narration_text: So the chart lands with both cells settled. Locking mechanism: 'supported — manual, page twelve.' Temperature sensor: 'no citation found,' flagged as a gap on purpose. Here's the trade-off baked into the design. A filled cell doesn't decide the case — a citation can be weak, or cover only part of the element. And a gap doesn't decide it either — it isn't proof the element fails, only proof no evidence has turned up yet. The output isn't a verdict. It's a map of exactly where to look next.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- the two rows resolve, then split into 'filled != proven' and 'gap != failed'

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS -- filled != proven, gap != failed
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 TWO-ROW CHART RETURNS, identical placement, both cells now settled: locking-mechanism cell reads 'SUPPORTED -- MANUAL, P.12', temperature-sensor cell reads 'NO CITATION FOUND' under its GAP tag. It then splits into two cards: left reads 'a citation can be weak or partial' beneath 'FILLED != PROVEN'; right reads 'no evidence found YET' beneath 'GAP != FAILED', connected only by a dashed line labelled 'shows where to look next'.

beats.narration_text: The point of a claim chart isn't a full grid -- it's a pin cite for what's supported, and a flag, element by element, for what's missing.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini: I want to check whether a document actually supports a set of claims — element by element, not overall. Take this list of elements and this source document. For each element, quote the exact passage that supports it and pin-cite the page and line. If nothing in the document matches, flag it as a gap. Don't guess. Don't stretch a nearby passage to fill the cell. Return a two-column table: element, then either the pin cite or the gap flag. Go deeper: what's the weakest cite that made it in, and what would a follow-up document need to say to close a gap without stretching the language you already have?

llm_exercise.prompt: I want to check whether a document actually supports a set of claims — element by element, not overall. Take this list of claim elements: [paste each element on its own line]. And this source document: [paste the document]. For each element, quote the exact passage that supports it and pin-cite the location (page and line, or paragraph number). If no passage in the document supports an element, mark that cell 'no citation found' as a gap — don't guess, and don't stretch a nearby passage to fill it. Return the result as a two-column table: element, then either the pin-cited quote or the gap flag.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: take the elements that came back with pin cites and stress-test each one — could the citation be read to cover only part of the element? What's the weakest cite in the chart, and what would a follow-up document need to say to close a gap without stretching the language you already have?
